The counts were supplied by DEWR to the Ombudsman. Later scale estimates come from secondary reporting of DEWR figures and Senate estimates evidence, not from a primary transcript.
facts: Under the Targeted Compliance Framework, when a Services Australia decision-maker is not satisfied a job seeker has a reasonable excuse and records the failure, the computer system automatically cancels the income support payment. [S86 p. 15]

An April 2022 amendment to s 42AF(2) of the Social Security (Administration) Act 1999 required decision-makers to decide whether to cancel a payment even where there was no reasonable excuse. [S86 p. 15]
After the amendment the system kept cancelling payments without reflecting the need for that discretionary decision, and decision-makers did not make it. [S86 p. 16]

The DEWR Secretary told the Ombudsman that cancellations had occurred automatically without consideration of job seekers' circumstances, affecting 964 job seekers; a further 45 received automated cancellations after the decision to pause cancellations, when they should not have. [S86 p. 3]
The Ombudsman found the s 42AF(2) cancellations were not lawful and formed the opinion that the agencies' actions were contrary to law. [S86 pp. 5, 15]

An independent review completed in June 2025 found that assurance could not be provided on the integrity, effectiveness or appropriateness of decisions produced by the TCF IT system in its current form. [S86 pp. 16 to 17]
The error went undetected from April 2022 until September 2023, and DEWR took almost 10 months after that to pause the cancellations in July 2024. [S86 p. 31]

On 19 October 2026 DEWR said it had begun inviting people who may be eligible for compensation for incorrect cancellations, that two paused provisions would resume on 26 October 2026, and that s 42AF(2) cancellations stay paused until further safeguards are in place, expected in the first quarter of 2027. [S87]

Government News reported that DEWR estimated in March 2025 that 10,000 jobseeker payments were unlawfully or wrongfully reduced or cancelled, and that a Senate estimates hearing in June 2026 heard the number of claimants affected was "in the vicinity" of 30,000. [S96]
published.incident_date: April 2022 to July 2024, with 45 further automated cancellations after the pause
published.incident_date_basis: The Ombudsman dates the unlawful s 42AF(2) cancellations from April 2022 to the 4 July 2024 pause; the 45 later cancellations followed the Secretary's pause decision.
inferences: Recording a failure and cancelling the payment were joined into one system step, so the decision the law required had no point at which a person could make it.
The cancellations after the pause show the system kept acting after the authority to cancel had been withdrawn.

The later estimates of 10,000 and about 30,000 cover payments unlawfully or wrongfully reduced or cancelled, a wider measure than the 964 s 42AF(2) cancellations the Ombudsman counted, so the two figures are not directly comparable.

facts: The respondent's counsel wrote to the appellant's counsel relying on Marriage of Twigg (1984) 34 Cal.3d 926 and Marriage of Teegarden (1995) 33 Cal.App.4th 1572; neither case exists as cited. [S91 p. 3]
A court commissioner sitting as temporary judge approved and signed a proposed order, drafted by the appellant's counsel, that cited both fictitious cases and denied pet custody. [S91 pp. 4 to 5]

In the Court of Appeal, the respondent's counsel cited the same cases in opposing reinstatement of the appeal, and after the appellant said they were invented, insisted Twigg was a valid published precedent and supplied reporter citations and a decision date the court found were also fictitious. [S91 pp. 5, 18 to 19]
Twigg came from a Reddit article by a non-attorney blogger, and the court described the fictional Teegarden case as apparently generated by AI. [S91 pp. 8, 18]

At oral argument counsel said she had no paid legal research subscription and was using other online resources including AI, and conceded she may have obtained fictitious information about Twigg and Teegarden using AI tools. [S91 p. 9]

The court held it is an abuse of discretion for a court to rely in material part on fictional case authorities, but found the appellant forfeited the claim because his own counsel drafted and submitted the order without objecting. [S91 pp. 10 to 11]
The court stated that it is particularly important for an attorney to verify the citations in any proposed order submitted for signature by the court. [S91 p. 13]

The court ordered the respondent's counsel to pay USD 5,000 in sanctions, directed the clerk to forward the opinion to the State Bar of California, and ordered counsel to report the sanction herself. [S91 p. 20]

facts: The respondent filed his Answer to the SRA's disciplinary allegations on 12 March 2026, and on 8 April 2026 the SRA's counsel identified incorrect citations and citations that did not reflect the stated legal propositions. [S92 para 19.2]
The SRA drew the errors to his attention on 8 April 2026 and directed him to Ayinde v Haringey LBC, the leading judgment on unchecked AI-generated legal arguments. [S92 para 19.3]
His reply of 9 April 2026, which purported to correct the errors, was itself drafted using generative AI and contained further false material. [S92 para 19.4]
On 13 April 2026 he accepted that the 9 April email had been produced with AI and contained inaccuracies, and said he could not provide copies of the authorities he relied on. [S92 para 19.5]

The Answer gave a 2015 case a 2020 citation it does not bear, gave another case a citation belonging to an unrelated intellectual property case, and cited two real cases for propositions they do not support. [S92 para 19.40]
He accepted that the Answer was prepared by AI software involving large language models, apologised, and said he had no intention to mislead. [S92 para 19.42]

The Tribunal found the allegations proved in respect of citing non-existent cases and incorrect legal propositions, assessed his culpability as very high because the conduct was repeated after the errors were explained, and said it would have imposed the same sanction had this allegation stood alone. [S92 paras 8.2, 19.50, 28.12, 28.16]

The Tribunal ordered that he be struck off the Register of Foreign Lawyers, with no order as to costs, and recorded that this was the first time a lawyer's use of AI in legal proceedings had been litigated before it. [S92 paras 8.3, 30]
The order is subject to an appeal to the High Court by the respondent and remains in force pending the High Court's decision. [S93]

facts: In June 2025 teachers, professors, students, parents and organizations filed a pre-enforcement challenge to Mississippi House Bill 1193, a law restricting diversity, equity and inclusion programs in public education. [S97 pp. 2 to 3, 5]

The temporary restraining order entered on 20 July 2025 named as plaintiffs eleven individuals and organizations who had never been party to the case, named two officials who were not sued, and referenced declarations of four individuals who do not appear in the record and may not exist. [S97 pp. 5 to 7]

The order misquoted the statute as applying to terms including "critical race theory" and "institutional bias", which do not appear in its text, and claimed without evidence that institutions had already cancelled programs because of the law. [S97 pp. 6 to 7]

After the state defendants pointed out the errors on 22 July 2025, the court replaced the order with a corrected version backdated to 20 July, denied a request to restore the original to the docket, and called the inaccuracies clerical. [S97 pp. 5, 7]
In a letter, the district judge acknowledged the errors and said a law clerk had used AI to assist in drafting an earlier version of the order that was docketed by mistake. [S97 p. 7]

At oral argument in the Fifth Circuit it was discovered that the corrected order cited "Cousins v. School Bd. of City of Norfolk", a Fourth Circuit case that does not exist and that the court called an apparent AI hallucination. [S97 p. 8]
The preliminary injunction entered on 18 August 2025 generally incorporated the corrected order's discussion and analysis by reference. [S97 pp. 5, 8]

On 22 October 2026 the Fifth Circuit vacated the preliminary injunction and directed the Chief Judge of the Southern District of Mississippi to assign the case to a different district judge. [S97 pp. 3 to 4, 27]

published.evidence_note: Primary Ombudsman investigation report states how the automated decisions are made, that the law allows no override, and the finding of unreasonable administration; the department's response is printed in the report. The Ombudsman did not assess whether the algorithm's outcomes are clinically correct, and the department disputes the finding on risk assessment. Appeal counts come from ABC News reporting.
facts: After an assessor completes the assessment questions, the IAT's algorithms decide whether the older person is eligible for the Commonwealth Home Support Program or the Support at Home program and, for Support at Home, set the funding classification and priority category. [S113 pp. 5 to 6]

The Ombudsman states that under the law these automated decisions cannot be overridden and changed, even if they are clinically inappropriate, and that a human decision-maker does not decide these matters. [S113 p. 6]

Support at Home funding has eight annual classification levels, from $10,731.00 to $78,106.35, and the priority category indicates how long the person is likely to wait, from under a month for urgent to 7 to 8 months for standard. [S113 Part 1]

The Ombudsman found the department implemented the IAT in its current form without any meaningful risk assessment, evaluation or analysis, despite the obvious risks of automated decision-making that does not allow human override. [S113 p. 12]

The Ombudsman found that the IAT appears to have been built with an override mechanism, but there is no mechanism at law to override and change automated decisions considered clinically inappropriate. [S113 p. 12]

Until the Act and the Rules were introduced in October 2025, the department had been incorrectly advising assessment providers and the public that automated IAT outcomes could be changed. [S113 pp. 12 to 13]

The Ombudsman formed the opinion that the department's administration of the Single Assessment System, including the implementation of the IAT, has been unreasonable, and said a reasonable person would lack confidence that the system is fair and consistent. [S113 pp. 11 to 12]

The Ombudsman did not assess the clinical appropriateness of the algorithm and states that its findings do not establish that the algorithm in fact produces clinically inappropriate outcomes. [S113 pp. 11 to 12]

The Ombudsman recommended a bill to let assessment delegates substitute their own decision for an automated IAT decision; the department noted this recommendation, pointing to the government's planned escalation pathway, and did not accept it. [S113 recommendation 1 and agency response]

ABC News reported that hundreds of people have appealed the algorithm's decisions, a more than five-fold increase on appeals in the previous year, and that the government passed legislation the week before the report for an escalation pathway in exceptional circumstances. [S114]

The Minister for Aged Care said the escalation pathway lets cases that cannot be appropriately assessed with the IAT be escalated to an alternate clinically informed approach, and that it is being implemented on 11 January. [S115]

published.incident_date_basis: The department's response in the report states the IAT and its algorithms were introduced on 1 November 2025; the Ombudsman reports that the law still allows no override.
inferences: The assessor's judgement shapes the inputs, while the scoring rules make the decision on funding and priority, leaving no point at which a person can lawfully change the result.

The escalation pathway covers exceptional or complex cases, which is narrower than the general substitution power the Ombudsman recommended, so most automated decisions remain without a human override.
The minister did not state the year for 11 January; given the timing of the interview, it appears to mean January 2027.
